title: Evaluation — FID, CLIP Score, Human Preference

questions.question: Which combination covers the three main evaluation axes in this lesson?
options: Resolution, batch size, and checkpoint size
Training loss, parameter count, and latency
Precision, recall, and classification accuracy
Sample quality, prompt adherence, and human preference
questions.explanation: FID estimates sample-distribution quality, CLIP score estimates prompt adherence, and blinded pairwise comparisons measure human preference.

questions.question: Why should FID normally be computed with a large sample set?
options: Inception-v3 cannot process small batches
Finite-sample mean and covariance estimates are noisy and bias the score
CLIP embeddings require exactly 10,000 prompts
Elo ratings are undefined below 10,000 comparisons
questions.explanation: FID depends on estimated feature means and covariances. Small samples make those estimates noisy, often yielding a positive FID even when both samples come from the same distribution and potentially distorting model rankings.

questions.question: What does CLIP score primarily measure for a generated image and its prompt?
options: The generator's likelihood loss
The probability that a human judge prefers the image
Fréchet distance between their pixel distributions
Cosine similarity between their CLIP image and text embeddings
questions.explanation: CLIP score uses cosine similarity between the generated image's CLIP embedding and the prompt's CLIP text embedding.

questions.question: Why can a strong CLIP score fail to prove that a model follows a complex prompt correctly?
options: CLIP has compositional blind spots and can be inflated by prompt wording
CLIP accepts only grayscale images
CLIP cannot compare image and text embeddings
CLIP score always decreases as visual quality improves
questions.explanation: CLIP can miss attribute and spatial relationships, while phrases such as 'high quality' can raise the score without improving true image-text binding.

questions.question: Which report provides the strongest evidence that a new image generator beats its baseline?
options: A higher Elo score on prompts seen during training
A lower FID from 1,000 samples and one seed
Matched-sample metrics, blinded preferences, and qualitative failure analysis
A higher CLIP score on hand-picked short prompts
questions.explanation: Triangulating distribution quality, prompt adherence, blinded preference, and qualitative failures is stronger because every individual metric has exploitable blind spots.

questions.question: A team evaluates artwork far outside ImageNet's domain. How should it address standard FID's limitation?
options: Report only the generator's training loss
Keep Inception features but reduce the sample count
Replace the held-out real set with generated images
Use a domain-appropriate extractor or a complementary metric such as CMMD
questions.explanation: Standard FID inherits the biases of ImageNet-trained Inception features. A domain-appropriate representation or a complementary CLIP-feature metric is more informative.
